groups.name: NSAID pain reliever
groups.summary: NSAIDs reduce blood flow to the kidneys. Regular or high-dose use can cause kidney injury, especially with dehydration, older age, heart failure or existing kidney disease. The National Kidney Foundation advises people with CKD to avoid them.
groups.ask: If you use this often, ask your doctor whether a different pain option is safer for your kidneys.

groups.name: Aspirin
groups.summary: Low-dose aspirin prescribed for heart protection is generally considered acceptable. High doses used for pain behave like other NSAIDs and can strain the kidneys.
groups.ask: Ask your doctor whether your aspirin dose is right for your kidney health.

groups.name: Lithium
groups.summary: Long-term lithium use can affect kidney function. Doctors check kidney blood tests regularly while you take it.
groups.ask: Keep up with the blood tests your doctor orders. Never stop lithium on your own.

groups.name: Aminoglycoside or similar antibiotic
groups.summary: These antibiotics are known to be hard on the kidneys. They are usually given in a hospital, with drug levels and kidney function monitored.
groups.ask: Make sure your care team knows about any kidney concerns before treatment.

groups.name: Proton pump inhibitor (acid reducer)
groups.summary: Long-term use of these acid reducers has been linked in studies to a higher risk of kidney disease. Short courses are generally considered low risk.
groups.ask: If you've taken this for months or years, ask your doctor whether you still need it.

groups.name: Antiviral
groups.summary: Some antivirals can affect the kidneys, especially at high doses or with dehydration. Doctors often adjust the dose based on kidney function.
groups.ask: Drink enough water and make sure your doctor knows your latest kidney test results.

groups.name: Immune-suppressing or chemotherapy medicine
groups.summary: These medicines can affect kidney function, so kidney blood tests are part of routine monitoring.
groups.ask: Keep up with scheduled lab tests and report any swelling or changes in urination.

groups.name: Metformin (diabetes)
groups.summary: Metformin does not damage the kidneys, and controlling diabetes protects them. Because the kidneys clear metformin, the dose may need to change if kidney function drops.
groups.ask: Ask your doctor to check your eGFR at least once a year while you take metformin.

groups.name: Diuretic (water pill)
groups.summary: Diuretics help control blood pressure and swelling. They can cause dehydration or changes in potassium, so doctors check blood tests from time to time.
groups.ask: Tell your doctor if you feel dizzy, very thirsty, or are sick with vomiting or diarrhea.

groups.name: Trimethoprim / sulfamethoxazole
groups.summary: This antibiotic can raise potassium and creatinine levels, and the dose may be lowered for people with reduced kidney function.
groups.ask: Drink plenty of fluids and tell your prescriber about any kidney concerns.

groups.name: IV bone medicine
groups.summary: Intravenous bone-strengthening medicines can affect the kidneys, so kidney function is checked before each dose.
groups.ask: Make sure kidney tests are done before your infusion.

groups.name: Sodium phosphate laxative
groups.summary: Sodium phosphate bowel preps and enemas have caused serious kidney injury (acute phosphate nephropathy), and the FDA has warned about them.
groups.ask: Ask your doctor about a different bowel prep if you have any kidney risk factors.

groups.name: ACE inhibitor (blood pressure)
groups.summary: ACE inhibitors are often prescribed to protect the kidneys, especially for people with diabetes or protein in the urine. They can raise potassium, so doctors check blood tests.
groups.ask: Keep taking it as prescribed and keep up with your lab tests.

groups.name: ARB (blood pressure)
groups.summary: ARBs are often prescribed to slow kidney damage from diabetes and high blood pressure. They can raise potassium, so doctors monitor blood tests.
groups.ask: Keep taking it as prescribed and keep up with your lab tests.

groups.name: SGLT2 inhibitor
groups.summary: Large clinical trials showed these medicines slow the decline of kidney function in many people with CKD, with or without diabetes.
groups.ask: Stay well hydrated and follow your doctor's guidance on sick days.

groups.name: Finerenone
groups.summary: Finerenone is approved to lower the risk of kidney decline in adults with CKD and type 2 diabetes.
groups.ask: Your doctor will check potassium levels while you take it.

groups.name: GLP-1 medicine
groups.summary: In a large trial of people with type 2 diabetes and CKD, semaglutide lowered the risk of serious kidney outcomes.
groups.ask: Keep taking it as prescribed and report severe nausea or vomiting, which can dehydrate you.

supplements.name: Aristolochic acid herbs
supplements.summary: Herbs containing aristolochic acid cause severe kidney damage and cancer. The FDA warns consumers not to use them.
supplements.ask: Stop and talk to a doctor if any product you use lists these ingredients.

supplements.name: Creatine supplement
supplements.summary: Creatine raises blood creatinine, which can make kidney tests look worse. It is not recommended for people with kidney disease.
supplements.ask: Tell your doctor you take creatine before any kidney blood test.

supplements.name: High-dose vitamin C
supplements.summary: Very high doses of vitamin C can increase oxalate and the risk of kidney stones.
supplements.ask: Stick to recommended amounts unless your doctor advises otherwise.

supplements.name: Licorice root
supplements.summary: Large amounts of real licorice can raise blood pressure and lower potassium.
supplements.ask: Avoid large amounts if you have high blood pressure or kidney concerns.
